rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.2-2.6 and 3 - a 2-year randomised block field experiment (2018-2019) in a wolfberry orchard on the Tibetan Plateau with three treatments (CK, MF, MR), measuring soil water content, soil water and xylem delta-18O, fine root length density, yield and WUE.
rows.notes: All three treatments use surface drip irrigation; the comparison is film mulch (flat or ridge-furrow) versus no mulch under drip, not DIPM versus traditional (non-drip) irrigation as the passage claims. Per the rating rules a mulch-versus-no-mulch trial under drip is evidence about mulch, not drip. What the study shows: soil water content across 0-100 cm was higher under MF and MR than CK by 30.2% and 37.1% on average (Section 3.2, Fig. 3); soil temperature increases under mulch are referred to only via supplementary Table S3; soil nutrient availability was not measured by treatment (Table 1 is site baseline only). Soil moisture result was by gravimetric sampling only, single site, single crop, plot scale.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.2-2.6 and 3 - own 2-year field experiment with three management treatments, fine root sampling (Section 2.3, Fig. 2), isotope-based water source partitioning (Fig. 5) and yield/WUE (Table 4).
rows.notes: The study does report that fine root length density in the shallow layer was significantly lower under CK (drip, no mulch) than under MF and MR (drip plus full film mulch), with FRLD order MR > MF > CK (Section 3.4, Fig. 2), and that mulched trees used more shallow-layer water (Section 3.3, Fig. 5). However, the comparator is drip without mulch, not traditional irrigation, so the result is evidence about film mulch/ridge-furrow under drip rather than about drip irrigation (DIPM versus traditional irrigation) as claimed. Nothing on emergence or growth-period length. Single site, single crop, plot scale; FRLD differences by Duncan letter groupings only.

notes: Supplementary tables (S1-S3) referenced for soil temperature and evaporation are not included in the provided text.
